attachments.origin_landmark: pubis, ischial spine, tendinous arch of the obturator fascia
attachments.insertion_landmark: coccyx, anococcygeal ligament, perineal body (puborectalis forms a U-shaped sling around the anorectal junction rather than a bony insertion)

innervation.root_levels: S2-S4 (pudendal nerve + direct sacral branches, 'nerve to levator ani')

functional_compartments.name: Puborectalis
functional_compartments.function_note: U-shaped sling passing posterior to the anorectal junction (no posterior bony attachment); tonic contraction maintains the anorectal angle central to fecal continence -- the most functionally distinct of the muscle's three parts.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) -- standard traditional 3-part division (puborectalis/pubococcygeus/iliococcygeus); Kearney R, Sawhney R, DeLancey JOL (2004) Obstet Gynecol 104(1):168-173 -- origin-insertion analysis of levator ani (note: that paper's own conclusion favors a finer 5-way subdivision -- puboperineal/pubovaginal/puboanal/puborectal/iliococcygeal -- rather than this traditional 3-part scheme; the 3-part model is used here as the standard simplified teaching division per Gray's/Kenhub/TeachMeAnatomy, corrected from an earlier draft's over-attribution to Kearney/DeLancey specifically, caught by adversarial fact-check, see docs/VERIFICATION.md)

functional_compartments.name: Pubococcygeus
functional_compartments.function_note: Main sheet-like part, pubis to coccyx/anococcygeal raphe; the part most often assessed clinically for pelvic floor strength.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. functional_compartments.name: Iliococcygeus
functional_compartments.function_note: Thinnest, most posterolateral part, arising from the tendinous arch (rather than the pubis directly) and often largely aponeurotic.

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Two clinically described approaches, neither routinely ultrasound-guided: (1) digitally-guided transperineal -- the needle enters the skin 3-4 cm lateral to the anus, lateral to the outer border of the external anal sphincter, and is advanced toward the mid-rectum while the operator's other index finger, placed in the rectum, hooks and retracts the muscle and palpates the advancing needle tip near (not through) the rectal mucosa before injecting; (2) transvaginal submucosal -- injections placed submucosally into the lateral vaginal wall over puborectalis/pubococcygeus (often alongside bulbospongiosus) at the levels judged most tender on digital palpation.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Pelvic floor, deep to the perianal skin (transperineal route) or vaginal mucosa (transvaginal route); puborectalis and pubococcygeus are palpated directly per rectum or per vagina to confirm hypertonicity before injection.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Digital palpation of a tender, hypertonic muscle band on rectal or vaginal examination is both the diagnostic sign of levator ani syndrome and the guide for needle placement; there is no consistent ultrasound landmark used across the published technique, in contrast to most other muscles in this atlas.
structures_at_risk: rectal mucosa, immediately medial to the transperineal needle path -- the finger-in-rectum technique exists specifically to avoid perforating it
anal canal and external anal sphincter, superficial/medial to the puborectalis injection points
pudendal neurovascular bundle, running in the ischioanal fossa lateral to the injection sites
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Botulinum toxin for levator ani syndrome/chronic pelvic pain has genuine but mixed evidence: uncontrolled series report good-to-partial response in roughly half to two-thirds of patients (e.g. 40 U/side digitally-guided, up to 8 repeat treatments), while most randomized placebo-controlled trials (e.g. 80 U onabotulinumtoxinA into paired puborectalis/pubococcygeus, Abbott et al. 2006) show no significant difference from saline on primary pain outcomes despite some positive secondary/exploratory measures -- a genuinely unresolved evidence base recorded here rather than presented as settled.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Ooijevaar RE et al. (2019) Tech Coloproctol 23(3):239-244, doi:10.1007/s10151-019-01945-8 -- digitally-guided transperineal technique and dosing, 113 patients (PubMed); Desai SA, Shah B, Kroumpouzos G (2024) Int J Womens Dermatol 10(4):e186, doi:10.1097/JW9.0000000000000186 -- transvaginal submucosal technique for vaginismus targeting bulbospongiosus/pubococcygeus/puborectalis (PubMed); Karp BI, Stratton P (2025) Toxicon 258:108336, doi:10.1016/j.toxicon.2025.108336 -- review summarizing RCT evidence (including Abbott et al. 2006) as equivocal despite positive uncontrolled series (PubMed)
